p.src: The tale tells how Grand Marshal Gao asked Huyan Zhuo, “Whom do you recommend to serve as vanguard, General?” Huyan Zhuo reported, “I recommend Han Tao, the military training commissioner of Chenzhou. He is a native of the Eastern Capital and once qualified through the military examinations. He wields a jujube-wood lance and is known as the ‘Ever-Victorious General.’ He can serve as chief vanguard. There is another man, Peng Qi, the military training commissioner of Yingzhou. He too is from the Eastern Capital, the son of a family that has produced generals for generations. He wields a three-pointed, double-edged blade and is outstanding in arms; men call him the ‘General of the Heavenly Eye.’ He can serve as deputy vanguard.” Grand Marshal Gao was delighted to hear this. “With Generals Han and Peng as our vanguards, why should we fear those mad bandits?” That same day, at the Palace Commandant’s headquarters, Grand Marshal Gao authorized two dispatches and ordered the Privy Council to send messengers through the night to Chenzhou and Yingzhou, summoning Han Tao and Peng Qi to hurry to the capital. Within ten days, both generals reached the capital and went straight to the Palace Commandant’s headquarters, where they paid their respects to the grand marshal and Huyan Zhuo. The next day, Grand Marshal Gao led them all to the imperial drill ground to display their martial skills. After completing the troop inspection, they returned to the Palace Commandant’s headquarters and conferred with officials of the Privy Council on weighty military affairs. Grand Marshal Gao asked, “How many troops do your three commands have in all?” Huyan Zhuo replied, “The cavalry of the three commands numbers five thousand; with the infantry, the total reaches ten thousand.” Grand Marshal Gao said, “You three are to return personally to your prefectures, select three thousand elite cavalry and five thousand infantry, agree upon a day to march, and go suppress Liangshan Marsh.” Huyan Zhuo reported, “The cavalry and infantry of these three commands are all thoroughly trained men, strong soldiers mounted on sturdy horses, so Your Excellency need have no concern. I fear only that their armor and uniforms are incomplete. If that should delay the appointed date, we would be liable to punishment; I beg Your Excellency to grant us more time.” Grand Marshal Gao said, “If that is the case, you three may go to the capital’s armory and, without restriction as to quantity, choose whatever uniforms, armor, helmets, and swords you require and draw them for your use. See that the troops and horses are properly equipped and ready to meet the enemy. On the day the army marches, I shall send an officer to inspect it myself.” Having received these orders, Huyan Zhuo took men to the armory to draw the supplies. Huyan Zhuo selected three thousand suits of iron armor, five thousand sets of cured-leather horse armor, three thousand bronze and iron helmets, two thousand long spears, one thousand rolling-bladed swords, countless bows and arrows, and more than five hundred fire-cannon and iron-cannon frames, and had them all loaded onto carts. On the day of their departure, Grand Marshal Gao also allotted them three thousand warhorses. Each of the three generals was rewarded with gold, silver, and bolts of silk, while all the troops received provisions and bounty. Huyan Zhuo, Han Tao, and Peng Qi each submitted a written pledge of certain victory, took leave of Grand Marshal Gao and the officials of the Privy Council, mounted their horses, and headed for Runingzhou. Nothing noteworthy occurred along the way.

p.src: Meanwhile, a far-ranging scout from Liangshan Marsh rode straight to the main stronghold and reported the news. In the Hall of Righteous Assembly, Chao Gai and Song Jiang sat in the center, the strategist Wu Yong above them, and the Daoist Gongsun Sheng below, while all the chieftains congratulated Chai Jin and feasted throughout the day. Then came the report: “‘Double Clubs’ Huyan Zhuo of Runingzhou is leading an army here to make war upon us.” They all began discussing how to meet the enemy. Wu Yong said, “I have heard that this man is a direct descendant of Huyan Zan, the famed general of Hedong and a meritorious founding minister. He is highly accomplished in arms and wields two bronze clubs, so no one can approach him. We must first send a general skilled in campaigning and bold in battle to oppose him with force, and then capture him by strategy.” Before he had finished speaking, ‘Black Whirlwind’ Li Kui cried, “I’ll go with you and seize that rogue!” Song Jiang said, “How could you be sent? I have my own dispositions. Let ‘Thunderbolt’ Qin Ming lead the first formation; ‘Panther Head’ Lin Chong the second; ‘Little Li Guang’ Hua Rong the third; ‘Ten Feet of Steel’ Hu Sanniang the fourth; and ‘Sickly Yuchi’ Sun Li the fifth. After each of the five forward formations has fought in turn, it is to wheel around like a spinning wheel and become the rear guard. I shall personally lead ten brothers and bring up the rear with the main body. The five generals of the left wing shall be Zhu Tong, Lei Heng, Mu Hong, Huang Xin, and Lü Fang; The five generals of the right wing shall be Yang Xiong, Shi Xiu, Ou Peng, Ma Lin, and Guo Sheng. On the waterways, let Li Jun, Zhang Heng, Zhang Shun, and the three Ruan brothers take boats and stand ready to support us.” He then ordered Li Kui and Yang Lin to divide the infantry into two forces and lie in ambush, ready to give support. Once Song Jiang had made all his assignments, Qin Ming promptly led the vanguard down the mountain and formed a battle line on the broad, open plain. Although it was winter, the weather was pleasantly mild. After waiting for a day, they saw the government army approaching. In the vanguard, the ‘Ever-Victorious General’ Han Tao led his troops in erecting a fortified camp. There was no fighting that night.

p.src: At daybreak the next morning, the two armies drew up against each other. After three rolls of the painted drums, the warriors rode out before the battle lines. Qin Ming sat on horseback with his wolf-toothed club held crosswise. When the banners at the opposing line parted, the vanguard commander Han Tao reined in his horse with his spear leveled and cursed him: “The imperial army has come, yet instead of surrendering at once, you still dare resist! You are courting death! I shall fill in your marsh, trample Liangshan flat, capture every one of you rebels alive, haul you to the capital, and hack you into ten thousand pieces!” Qin Ming was hot-tempered by nature. Hearing this, he answered not a word, but spurred his horse, brandished his wolf-toothed club, and charged straight at Han Tao. Han Tao leveled his spear, urged his horse forward, and engaged Qin Ming. They fought for more than twenty bouts. Han Tao, feeling his strength fail, was just about to flee when the commander of the center, Huyan Zhuo, arrived behind him. Seeing that Han Tao could not prevail against Qin Ming, he brandished his twin clubs, urged forward the imperial gift beneath him—the Black Steed That Treads the Snow—and came roaring and shouting to the front of the lines. When Qin Ming saw him, he was about to engage Huyan Zhuo, but Lin Chong, the “Panther Head,” arrived with the second contingent and called, “Commander Qin, rest awhile! Watch me fight him for three hundred bouts, and then we shall see!” Lin Chong leveled his serpent spear and charged straight at Huyan Zhuo. Qin Ming wheeled his troops around the left and withdrew behind the hillside. Huyan Zhuo then fought Lin Chong, the two of them evenly matched: spear and clubs flashing back and forth like a ball of flowers, clubs and spear crossing like a cluster of brocade. They fought for more than fifty bouts, with neither gaining the advantage. When the third contingent under Hua Rong, the “Little Li Guang,” arrived, he shouted from the gate of the formation, “General Lin, rest awhile! Watch me capture this rogue!” Lin Chong turned his horse and withdrew. Huyan Zhuo, having seen how formidable Lin Chong’s martial skill was, also returned to his own lines. Lin Chong wheeled his own troops around and led them behind the hillside, leaving Hua Rong to ride out with his spear leveled. By then Huyan Zhuo’s rear contingent had arrived. Peng Qi, the “Heaven-Eyed General,” held crosswise his three-pointed, double-edged blade with four apertures and eight rings, spurred his yellow-flowered thousand-li horse Wuming, and rode out to curse Hua Rong: “A rebel and traitor against the realm is scarcely worth mentioning! Come and settle victory or defeat with me!” Hua Rong flew into a rage. Without answering, he crossed horses with Peng Qi. After they had fought for more than twenty bouts, Huyan Zhuo saw Peng Qi weakening, so he spurred his horse, flourished his clubs, and charged straight at Hua Rong. They had fought fewer than three bouts when the fourth contingent under Hu Sanniang, the “Ten-Foot Green Snake,” arrived. She shouted, “General Hua, rest awhile! Watch me capture this rogue!” Hua Rong likewise led his troops around to the right and withdrew beneath the hillside. Before Peng Qi’s contest with the “Ten-Foot Green Snake” was decided, the fifth contingent under Sun Li, the “Sick Yuchi,” had already arrived. He reined in before the formation and waited there, watching Hu Sanniang fight Peng Qi. Amid the shadows of battle dust and the gloom of murderous fury, one wielded a great pole-blade and the other twin sabers. After more than twenty bouts, the “Ten-Foot Green Snake” spread her two blades apart, turned her horse, and fled. Eager to win distinction, Peng Qi spurred after her. The “Ten-Foot Green Snake” hung her twin sabers from the saddle bow and drew from beneath her robe a red brocade lasso fitted with twenty-four golden hooks. Waiting until Peng Qi’s horse came near, she twisted around and cast the lasso into the air. Her aim was true; Peng Qi was caught unprepared and dragged straight from his horse. Sun Li shouted to his soldiers to rush forward together, and they seized Peng Qi. Huyan Zhuo was furious when he saw this and charged desperately forward to the rescue. The “Ten-Foot Green Snake” spurred out to meet him. Huyan Zhuo wished he could swallow the “Ten-Foot Green Snake” in a single gulp, yet after more than ten bouts he still could not quickly overcome her. Huyan Zhuo thought, “This wretched woman has traded so many bouts with me, and she is truly formidable!” Growing anxious and impatient, he deliberately showed an opening and let her come in. Then he brought both clubs sweeping down, pinning her twin sabers against her breast;

p.src: In the government ranks, Han Tao heard that Peng Qi had been lost. He went to the rear, mustered every soldier and horse, and led them all forward into the fray. Fearing they might break through, Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip. The ten chieftains led all their officers and men in a sweeping counterattack. The four columns behind them divided into two wings and closed in with a pincer attack. Seeing this, Huyan Zhuo hastily rallied his own troops and set each unit to hold off an attacker. Why could Song Jiang’s forces not win a complete victory? Because Huyan Zhuo’s formation consisted entirely of government chain-linked cavalry: the horses wore barding and the men iron armor. The horses’ armor left only their four hooves showing above the ground; the armored men left only their two eyes exposed. Though Song Jiang’s formation also had armored horses, their protection amounted only to red-tasseled face guards, bronze bells, and pheasant-tail ornaments. When arrows were shot from this side, the armor on the other side stopped them all. Moreover, every man among those three thousand cavalrymen carried a bow and arrows and shot straight back at them, so Song Jiang’s troops dared not approach. Song Jiang urgently ordered the gong sounded to recall his troops. Huyan Zhuo likewise withdrew more than twenty li and made camp.

Moreover, every man among those three thousand cavalrymen carried a bow and arrows and shot straight back at them, so Song Jiang’s troops dared not approach.
Song Jiang urgently ordered the gong sounded to recall his troops. Huyan Zhuo likewise withdrew more than twenty li and made camp.

The moment Song Jiang saw him, he rose, ordered the soldiers back, personally untied his bonds, helped him into the tent, and seated him in the place of a guest. Song Jiang then bowed to him. Peng Qi hastily returned the bow and said, “I am a captive and by rights should be put to death. Why, then, does the general treat me with the courtesy due a guest?” Song Jiang said, “We had nowhere that would shelter us, so we temporarily occupied the marsh as a refuge and have committed many offenses. Now that the court has dispatched you, General, to arrest us, we should properly have stretched out our necks and submitted to the bonds. p.src: That same day, Song Jiang had “Heaven-Eyed General” Peng Qi escorted to the main stronghold, where he was presented to Heavenly King Chao and kept within the stockade. Meanwhile, he rewarded the three armies and all the chieftains and deliberated over the military situation. Now Huyan Zhuo, after withdrawing his troops and making camp, conferred privately with Han Tao about how they might defeat the Liangshan Marsh stronghold. Han Tao said, “Today, when those rogues saw us driving our army forward, they rushed out in alarm to strike at us. Tomorrow, if we drive the entire cavalry force forward, we are certain to win a great victory.” Huyan Zhuo said, “I have already arranged matters just so. I merely wished to make sure that you and I were of one mind.” He immediately issued an order: “Form the three thousand cavalry horses into a single rank. Link them in groups of thirty with iron rings and chains. When the enemy appears, shoot arrows at long range and use spears at close quarters, charging straight into their ranks. The three thousand ‘chain-linked cavalry’ are to be secured in one hundred companies. Five thousand infantrymen will support them from the rear. Tomorrow, do not issue a challenge. You and I shall remain in the rear to supervise the battle. Once battle is joined, charge at them from three directions.” Their strategy settled, they marched out to battle at daybreak the following morning.

p.src: The next day, Song Jiang divided his troops and horses into five companies at the front, with ten commanders and the rear guard massed behind them, while two ambush forces took positions to left and right. Qin Ming took the lead and challenged Huyan Zhuo to come out and fight, but the opposing formation merely raised battle cries and did not engage. The five leading companies were all drawn up in a straight line before the formation: Qin Ming in the center, Lin Chong and “Ten Feet of Blue” on the left, and Hua Rong on the right, with Sun Li behind. Soon afterward, Song Jiang arrived with ten commanders, arraying rank upon rank of men and horses. When he examined the enemy formation, he saw about a thousand infantrymen merely beating drums and shouting, without a single man riding out to fight. Suspicious, Song Jiang secretly passed down an order: “Have the rear guard withdraw for now.” He then spurred his horse straight into Hua Rong’s company to survey the enemy. Suddenly, a rapid succession of cannon shots thundered from the enemy formation. The thousand infantrymen abruptly divided in two, releasing ‘chain-linked cavalry’ from three directions to charge straight at them. The wings loosed volleys of arrows, while the center bristled entirely with long spears. Song Jiang was greatly alarmed and hastily ordered his troops to shoot, but they were quite unable to withstand the assault. The thirty horses in each company galloped forward as one, so that not a single rider could help but advance. Those ‘chain-linked cavalry’ covered hill and field, charging wildly in every direction. At the sight of them, the five companies at the front broke and fled, unable to maintain their formation. The main force behind them could not check the rout, and every man fled for his life. Song Jiang hastily galloped away, protected by the ten commanders. A company of ‘chain-linked cavalry’ was already pursuing them from behind, but the ambush troops—Li Kui and Yang Lin—led their men charging out of the reeds and rescued Song Jiang. They fled to the water’s edge, where Li Jun, Zhang Heng, Zhang Shun, and the three Ruan brothers—the six naval commanders—had warships ready to receive them. Song Jiang hurried aboard and at once gave orders for the boats to split up and rescue the other chieftains. The ‘chain-linked cavalry’ pursued them right to the water’s edge and sent a hail of arrows after them, but the boats were protected by side shields, so no one was harmed. They hastily rowed to Duckbill Shoal and all went ashore. When they mustered the troops in the naval stockade, more than half their men had been lost, though fortunately all the chieftains were safe. Though they had lost some horses, they had all escaped with their lives. A short while later, Shi Yong, Shi Qian, Sun Xin, and Madam Gu came fleeing up the mountain and reported, “The infantry charged in and razed the inn buildings to the ground. Had the signal boats not come to our aid, we would all have been captured.” Song Jiang personally comforted them one by one. When the chieftains were counted, six had been struck by arrows: Lin Chong, Lei Heng, Li Kui, Shi Xiu, Sun Xin, and Huang Xin. Among the common soldiers, those wounded or carrying arrows in their bodies were beyond counting. When Chao Gai heard the news, he came down the mountain with Wu Yong and Gongsun Sheng to inquire after them. Song Jiang’s brow remained furrowed, and his face was clouded with worry. Wu Yong consoled him, saying, “Brother, do not grieve. Victory and defeat are both common in war. Why let it weigh on your mind? We shall devise another sound strategy to defeat the ‘chain-linked cavalry.’” Chao Gai then issued orders to the naval force, instructing them to secure the stockades and boats, guard the shoal, and remain vigilant night and day. He invited Song Gongming to go up the mountain and rest. Song Jiang refused to go up the mountain and remained stationed in the stockade at Duckbill Shoal, sending only the wounded chieftains up the mountain to recuperate.

A scout came to report: “The Eastern Capital has newly dispatched an artilleryman named Ling Zhen, known as ‘Heaven-Shaking Thunder.’ He is now setting up carriages at the water’s edge and preparing to fire cannon at our stockade.” Scholar Wu said, “That need not trouble us. For now, let us abandon the small stockade on Duckbill Shoal and see what method he uses to fire them. p.src: The six naval chieftains received their orders and divided into two groups. Li Jun and Zhang Heng first took forty or fifty strong swimmers in two swift boats and slipped quietly through the dense reeds; behind them, Zhang Shun and the three Ruan brothers followed in support with more than forty small boats. Li Jun and Zhang Heng then landed on the opposite bank, rushed to the gun carriages with a battle cry, and overturned them. The soldiers hurried to inform Ling Zhen. Taking the Wind-and-Fire cannons with him, Ling Zhen seized his spear, mounted his horse, and led more than a thousand men in pursuit. Li Jun and Zhang Heng led their men away. Ling Zhen pursued them to the reedy shoal, where he saw more than forty small boats drawn up in a single line, carrying altogether over a hundred naval troops. Li Jun and Zhang Heng had already leapt aboard. Deliberately leaving the boats where they were, they waited until the horsemen and foot soldiers drew near, then gave a shout and all jumped into the water. Ling Zhen’s troops had now arrived and rushed to seize the boats. Across the water, Zhu Tong and Lei Heng raised a clamor and beat their drums. Having captured many boats, Ling Zhen ordered all his soldiers aboard and launched an attack across the water. The boats had only just reached midstream when Zhu Tong and Lei Heng sounded their gongs on the bank. At once, forty or fifty naval troops surfaced from beneath the water and pulled out every stern plug, sending water surging into the boats. Those outside took advantage of the moment to overturn the boats, pitching all the soldiers into the water. Ling Zhen urgently tried to turn his boat back, but its rudder and oars had already been dragged beneath the water. Two chieftains surfaced on either side, seized the boat, and flipped it upside down, spilling Ling Zhen into the water. Ruan Xiaoer was waiting below the surface. He seized Ling Zhen in a tight embrace and dragged him straight to the opposite bank. Chieftains were already waiting on shore to receive him. They bound him with rope and escorted him up the mountain first. More than two hundred men were captured alive in the water; half the force drowned, and only a few escaped with their lives. Song Jiang came down to the second pass with all the chieftains of the stronghold to welcome him. On seeing Ling Zhen, he hurriedly untied him with his own hands and rebuked the others: “I told you to invite the commander courteously up the mountain. How could you treat him so rudely?” Ling Zhen bowed and thanked him for sparing his life. Song Jiang drank a cup with him, then took him by the hand and personally invited him up the mountain. When they reached the main stronghold, Ling Zhen saw that Peng Qi had already become one of its chieftains and fell silent. Peng Qi urged him: “Chieftains Chao and Song uphold justice on Heaven’s behalf and welcome men of valor. They await only an imperial amnesty, after which they intend to serve the state. Since we have come here, we can only submit to their command.” Song Jiang also spoke reassuringly to him, whereupon Ling Zhen replied: “I have no objection to serving here, but my aged mother, wife, and children are all in the capital. If anyone should learn of this, they will surely be put to death. What am I to do?” Song Jiang said, “Set your mind at ease. Within a fixed number of days, we shall bring them back to you, Commander.” Ling Zhen thanked him, saying, “If you can make such thorough arrangements for me, Chieftain, I could die with my eyes closed in peace.” Chao Gai said, “For now, have a banquet prepared to celebrate.”

p.src: The next day, all the chieftains gathered in a grand assembly in the hall. As they drank, Song Jiang discussed with the others how they might break the chain-linked cavalry. Just when no good plan could be found, Tang Long, the Golden-Money Spotted Leopard, rose and said: “Though I am a man of little ability, I would offer a plan. If we can obtain a certain kind of weapon and bring one elder cousin of mine here, we can defeat the chain-linked cavalry.” Scholar Wu immediately asked, “Brother, first tell us what kind of weapon is needed. And who is this kinsman of yours?” Tang Long, perfectly composed, stepped forward with clasped hands and named both the weapon and the man. And so it came to pass that four or five chieftains went straight to the capital, while more than three thousand cavalrymen met with deadly ruin. Indeed: the plan laid in the Jade Capital would capture the xiezhi; the scheme fulfilled at the Golden Pass would seize the suanni. What weapon and what man did Tang Long name before the assembled company? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
